title: London Particular
subtitle: Split pea and smoked bacon soup, thick and deeply savoury
excerpt: London Particular is a thick split pea and smoked bacon soup named after the dense, yellowish fogs that once choked the city. Dried split peas cook down into a velvety soup, with smoked bacon giving it depth and a faintly smoky character. It is one of the most satisfying soups in the British canon and requires almost no technique.
sourceNotes: London Particular was named by Charles Dickens in Bleak House (1852), where a character uses the term to describe the thick yellow fog of Victorian London. The soup is a direct equivalent of the fog in colour and density. It is documented in British cookbooks from the eighteenth century onwards.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Defrost and reheat gently, adding a splash of water or stock to loosen if needed.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch , it improves the next day and freezes well.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make 1 to 2 days ahead. Reheat gently on the hob.

content.text: London Particular is one of the easiest British soups to make: yellow split peas soften without pre-soaking and dissolve into a thick, creamy soup in about 90 minutes. The smoked bacon (lardons or rashers) goes in at the start to flavour the stock and is either left in or removed and crisped separately to serve on top. Season only at the end: the bacon and stock carry a lot of salt.

In a large pan, fry half the lardons over medium heat until they render their fat and become lightly crisp. Add {{onion}} chopped onion, {{carrot}} chopped carrot, and {{celery}} chopped celery. Cook for 5 minutes until softened. Add {{garlic}} of crushed garlic.

Add the rinsed split peas, the remaining lardons, {{stock-chicken}} of stock, the thyme, and the bay leaves. Bring to the boil, skim off any foam, then reduce to a steady simmer. Cook for 75 to 90 minutes until the peas have broken down into a thick, smooth soup. Remove the thyme and bay leaves.

Use a stick blender to blend most of the soup, leaving a little texture if preferred. Or blend completely for a smooth soup. Season carefully: the bacon adds considerable salt. Serve with crispy lardons on top and bread alongside.

items.symptom: The split peas have not broken down after 90 minutes
items.cause: Old dried peas take longer to soften. Very hard water can also slow cooking.
items.fix: Continue simmering until the peas are fully soft. You can also use a stick blender to help break them down even if they have not dissolved completely.

items.symptom: The soup is very thick and gluey
items.cause: The peas have reduced the soup more than intended.
items.fix: Add hot stock or water to thin to the consistency you prefer. Pea soup thickens significantly as it cools.

items.symptom: The soup is bland despite the bacon
items.cause: The peas absorbed the salt and the stock was mild.
items.fix: Season generously at the end with salt and black pepper. A small piece of ham hock cooked in the soup (and removed before blending) also builds depth.

items.symptom: The soup has a slightly floury texture
items.cause: The peas were undercooked and still grainy.
items.fix: Continue simmering. Split peas go from firm to smooth; there is no in-between. They need to be fully dissolved for the right texture.

content.text: London Particular was named for the dense, sulphurous yellow fogs that blanketed the city from the Industrial Revolution until the Clean Air Act of 1956 stopped them. The soup shares the fog's colour and density, which is presumably why a character in Bleak House reached for it as a description. It is a Victorian dish that has outlasted its Victorian city and remains one of the most warming and straightforward soups in the British repertoire.
